+\section{At a glance}
+
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty: easy.}  No step of the retained proof route is
+  in doubt.  The obstruction is that the error function claimed in the
+  statement of the combined-lines lemma of the Pauli basis analysis,
+  $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, is not delivered by either of the two
+  derivations printed in its source proof: one route establishes
+  $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$, the other would give
+  $m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and rests in addition on a distributional
+  decomposition that the stated sub-line lemma does not supply.  The
+  substance is deciding which error form the statement should carry and
+  confirming that the sole consumer tolerates it.
+  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib and mathematical inputs:} the
+  Cauchy--Schwarz inequality for state-dependent operator distances
+  (project-local, blueprint Chapter 12), mixture decompositions of
+  question distributions, and elementary averaging over restricted
+  line distributions; no new Mathlib surface beyond finite
+  expectations and inner-product estimates already used by the
+  low individual degree development.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight:} a \textbf{statement-level error-form
+  decision} plus about \textbf{one lemma interface} of checking that the
+  consumer absorbs an $m$ prefactor into its constants; the three chained
+  claims behind the retained route are ordinary Cauchy--Schwarz estimates,
+  on the order of \textbf{a few hundred lines} of formal proof in total
+  when that part of the development is reached.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split:} essentially \textbf{100\%
+  project-local}.  The estimates use only the project's state-dependent
+  distance calculus, the sub-line distribution, and elementary
+  probability on finite sets.
+  \item \textbf{Key inputs:} the combined point and line measurements and
+  the sub-line distribution of the Pauli basis analysis in
+  \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, and the error function of the classical soundness
+  theorem imported from \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}, into which the
+  corrected error form must be absorbed.  Tracked in \localissue{0002}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple of the Pauli basis
+test, $\ket{\hat\psi}$ is the expanded state of the projective strategy
+under analysis, succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, and all
+approximations are with respect to $\ket{\hat\psi}$.  For lines
+$\ell_X, \ell_Z$ in $\F_q^m$, the POVM $\{T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\}$,
+with outcomes pairs of polynomials of degree at most $md$ on the two
+lines, is the two-basis combined line measurement, and
+$\{\hat Q^{x,z}_{a,b}\}$ is the combined point measurement; their
+consistency errors are $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and
+$\delta_Q = \poly(\eps)$ respectively, and
+$\delta_{\mathrm{Line}} = \poly(\eps)$ is the line--point consistency
+error of the strategy.  The lemma under discussion asserts that a
+measurement $\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, built for each line $\ell$ in
+$\F_q^{2m+2}$, is $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$-consistent, on average over
+the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$, with the combined point
+measurement on the extended coordinates, together with the
+register-swapped counterpart.%
+\footnote{In the mirror of the source consulted here,
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}: the
+lemma statement, with the error form $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, is at
+lines~1020--1034 (label \path{lem:qld-4-13}); the central display with
+the first-route bound at lines~1134--1137
+(label \path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}); the three claims at
+lines~1140--1239 (labels \path{claim:17-1}--\path{claim:17-3}); the
+second-route conclusion $O(m^2\delta_P)$ at lines~1241--1245, preceded by
+a duplicated sentence whose second copy carries a malformed reference;
+the product-distribution estimate invoked there at lines~1055--1061
+(label \path{eq:qld-xz-lines-restricted}); and the sub-line lemma at
+lines~1063--1116 (label \path{lem:qld-sublines}).}
+The comparison involves four forms of the error function
+$\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}(\eps,m,d,q)$.
+\begin{enumerate}
+  \item \textbf{Source form.}
+  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = \poly(m^2\eps,\, md/q)$.  This is the form
+  printed in the statement.  Neither printed derivation supports it.
+  \item \textbf{Established form (first route).}
+  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}
+  = O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
+  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)$, a function of the form
+  $m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)$.
+  \item \textbf{Second-route form (conditional).}
+  $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = O(m^2 \delta_P)
+  = m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)$, conditional on a joint-law
+  decomposition that the sub-line lemma, as stated, does not provide.
+  \item \textbf{Consumer requirement.}  The unique consumer, the
+  polynomial-pair lemma, feeds $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$ into an error
+  of the form
+  $a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ imported
+  from \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}; any bound
+  $m^{O(1)} \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ is absorbed by enlarging $a$ and
+  shrinking $b$, so forms~2 and~3 both suffice downstream.
+\end{enumerate}
+
+\section{The source assertion and the two routes}
+
+The source proof in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} constructs $\hat Q^{\ell}_f$ by
+averaging, over a distribution $D$ on tuples $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$
+provided by its sub-line lemma, the pushforward of
+$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}$ along a combining map, and reduces the lemma to a
+bound on the scalar consistency defect
+\begin{equation}
+  \Lambda \,=\,
+  \E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
+  \E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
+  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
+  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
+  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
+  \ket{\hat\psi}\,,
+  \tag{\path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}}
+\end{equation}
+in which the point $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ is uniform on $\ell$ and the sum
+ranges over pairs of line polynomials.  The proof then bounds $\Lambda$
+twice, by different routes and with different results, and the printed
+record is internally inconsistent: the display introducing $\Lambda$
+asserts the first-route bound, while the closing lines assert the
+second-route bound as the operative one; the lemma statement claims a
+third form matching neither.
+
+\paragraph{The first route.}
+Three claims are chained.  The combined point measurement
+$\hat Q^{x,z}$ is replaced by the ordered product of the two point
+measurements at cost $\delta_Q^{1/2}$; the $X$-point factor is removed at
+cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$; and the remaining $Z$-point
+correlation is shown to be within
+$\sqrt{m}\,(\delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} + \eps^{1/4})$ of one.  The
+factors of $m$ enter through the mixture structure of the sub-line
+distribution: each restricted line distribution carries mixture weight
+$1/(2m)$ in the line-point distribution, so an average bounded by
+$\delta$ over the full distribution is bounded only by $2m\delta$ over a
+restricted component and by $4m^2\delta$ over a product of two
+components, and the Cauchy--Schwarz steps halve the exponents.  Chaining
+the claims gives
+\begin{equation*}
+  \Lambda \,=\, O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
+  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)
+  \,=\, m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)\,.
+\end{equation*}
+One intermediate assertion needs a harmless correction: the final line
+of the proof of the second claim asserts the bound
+$O(m^2 \delta_{\mathrm{Line}})$ for a consistency term that is close to
+one, rather than for its deficit.  Read as a bound on the deficit ---
+which is what the surrounding Cauchy--Schwarz argument requires and what
+the invoked line--point consistency provides after the mixture
+inflation --- the claim and its use are correct, with the square root of
+the deficit giving the stated cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$.
+
+\paragraph{The second route.}
+After the chain, the source restarts: it asserts that, by Property~2 of
+its sub-line lemma, $\Lambda$ is a mixture, over types
+$\mathrm{v}_1, \mathrm{v}_2 \in \{\mathrm{ALine}, \mathrm{DLine}\}$ and
+indices $i, j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, of terms
+\begin{equation*}
+  \E_{(\ell_X, x) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_1,i}}\
+  \E_{(\ell_Z, z) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_2,j}}
+  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
+  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
+  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
+  \ket{\hat\psi}
+\end{equation*}
+over two \emph{independently} sampled restricted line-point pairs,
+bounds each term by $O(m^2\delta_P)$ using the restricted-distribution
+consequence of the two-basis line lemma, and concludes
+$\Lambda = O(m^2\delta_P)$.  The invoked decomposition concerns the
+\emph{joint} law of the pair $((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z))$, where $x$ and
+$z$ are the two blocks of the single point sampled on $\ell$.  Property~2
+of the sub-line lemma does not assert this joint law: it asserts the
+component-wise product law of the pair of \emph{lines}
+$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, and the conditional uniformity of each point on its
+line separately --- equivalently, the laws of the two pairs
+$((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z'))$ and $((\ell_X, x'), (\ell_Z, z))$ in which
+the \emph{other} point is resampled independently.  These marginal
+statements are exactly what the first route's claims consume, each
+involving one point at a time; the joint decomposition used by the
+second route is a strictly stronger property and is not established by
+the lemma it is attributed to.
+
+\section{Why neither route yields the stated form}
+
+The stated error form is $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, a function of the two
+quantities $m^2\eps$ and $md/q$ that vanishes as both vanish.  The
+first-route bound is not dominated by any such function: along the
+scaling $\eps = m^{-4}$ with $q/(md) \to \infty$, both $m^2\eps = m^{-2}$
+and $md/q$ tend to $0$, while the term $m\,\eps^{1/4} = 1$ does not.
+Hence the established derivation supports no bound of the claimed form.
+The second-route bound, even granting the missing decomposition, carries
+the separate prefactor $m^2$: writing $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$
+with some fixed positive exponents, the contribution
+$m^2 (md/q)^{c}$ is not dominated by any vanishing function of $m^2\eps$
+and $md/q$, as the scaling $\eps = 0$, $md/q = m^{-2/c}$ shows, and the
+$\eps$-contribution fails similarly for sublinear exponents.  Neither
+observation asserts that the \emph{conclusion} of the lemma is false for
+some error function of the claimed form; the defect is that the printed
+proof does not deliver it.
+
+For orientation, the algebraic identity
+$m\,\eps^{1/2} = (m^2\eps)^{1/2}$ shows what a derivation of the claimed
+$\eps$-dependence would need: a chain that loses only square roots in the
+$\eps$-type quantities \emph{after} the restricted-distribution
+inflation would produce terms of the shape $(m^2\eps)^{1/2}$.  The
+printed chain loses fourth roots, through two nested Cauchy--Schwarz
+steps applied to already square-rooted quantities, and its
+$md/q$-dependence enters as $m\,\delta_P^{1/4}$, which the claimed form
+cannot absorb.
+
+\section{Candidate repairs}
+
+The following are candidate directions, with their open obligations; none
+of the routes below is claimed as established.
+
+\paragraph{Correcting the error form (recommended direction).}
+Adopt $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ ---
+concretely, the first-route bound --- as the operative error form.  Open
+obligations: (i)~verify that every consumer tolerates the prefactor; in
+the source and in the blueprint the only consumer is the polynomial-pair
+lemma, whose imported error
+$a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ absorbs
+$m^{O(1)}$ prefactors by enlarging $a$ and shrinking $b$, and this
+absorption must be carried out with explicit constants when the lemma is
+formalized; (ii)~record the correction against the source-labelled
+statement in accordance with the proof-gap protocol, rather than
+silently substituting the corrected form --- the blueprint currently
+retains the source statement and carries the corrected bound in the
+proof; (iii)~confirm the three chained claims at the required level of
+detail, including the corrected deficit reading of the second claim.
+
+\paragraph{Repairing the second route.}
+Strengthen Property~2 of the sub-line lemma to the joint product law: in
+each mixture component, the pairs $(\ell_X, x)$ and $(\ell_Z, z)$ are
+independent with the stated restricted-distribution laws.  The sampling
+procedure makes this plausible, since in each component the two pairs
+are built from disjoint collections of the independent ingredients (the
+two blocks of the uniform point, the direction blocks, and the fresh
+auxiliary choices).  Open obligations: (i)~state and prove the
+strengthened property for every component, including lines whose
+direction blocks vanish and degenerate to singletons; (ii)~re-derive the
+mixture decomposition of $\Lambda$ from the strengthened property;
+(iii)~note that even then the route delivers only
+$O(m^2\delta_P) = m^2 \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$, so this direction removes
+the unsupported step of the printed proof but still requires the
+error-form decision of the previous direction, with $m^2$ in place of
+$m$.
+
+\paragraph{Establishing the claimed form.}
+Re-derive the chain so that every factor of $m$ enters jointly with
+$\eps$ as $m^2\eps$, in the sense of the orientation identity above.
+Open obligations: (i)~find a chaining that avoids one of the two nested
+square-root losses, or prove restricted-distribution versions of the
+underlying consistency lemmas directly at their inflated errors;
+(ii)~handle the $md/q$-dependence, since a residual term
+$m (md/q)^{c}$ is incompatible with the claimed form for the current
+exponents.  No derivation along these lines is known here, and the
+direction may be infeasible; in that case the corrected error form of
+the first direction stands.
+
+\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
+
+The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} keeps the combined-lines lemma in
+its source shape, error form $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$ included, and marks
+in the proof that this form remains unproved: the proof derives the
+first route only, records the established bound
+$m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$, and uses that bound in the sequel.  The
+three claims are stated as separate lemmas with the corrected deficit
+assertion for the second; the sub-line lemma states Property~2 at the
+level of the two marginal laws and expressly disclaims the joint
+conditional law of the two points, so the blueprint statement does not
+license the second route; and the polynomial-pair lemma's proof absorbs
+the $m$ prefactor into the constants of the imported soundness error.  A
+chapter remark summarizes the discrepancy and cites this note.%
+\footnote{The blueprint statements are \path{lem:qld-4-13},
+\path{lem:qld-sublines}, \path{lem:claim-17-1}--\path{lem:claim-17-3},
+\path{lem:qld-4-7}, and the remark
+\path{rem:qld-4-13-source-defects}, all in
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex}.  No Lean
+declaration is currently linked to any of them.}
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+
+There is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma, together with an
+intermediate inconsistency: the printed proof asserts two different
+bounds for the same consistency defect, the first-route bound
+$O(m(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} +
+\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}))$ and the second-route bound
+$O(m^2\delta_P)$, the second resting on a joint-law decomposition that
+the sub-line lemma as stated does not supply; and the error form claimed
+in the lemma statement, $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, follows from neither.
+The first route is sound after a harmless deficit correction in its
+second claim and establishes $m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$.  The
+discrepancy is harmless downstream, since the sole consumer absorbs
+polynomial-in-$m$ prefactors into its constants.  The recommended
+resolution is to treat the corrected error form as operative while the
+source-labelled statement retains its printed form with the missing step
+explicitly tracked; strengthening the sub-line lemma to license the
+second route is optional, and no route to the claimed form is currently
+known.  We do not assert that the claimed form is false.
+

 \section{The classical low individual degree game}
 % Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
 \label{sec:ld-verifier}
 \label{sec:ld-game}
 
 The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

 We recall the Magic Square game of Mermin and Peres. It is a simple self-test for two EPR pairs, and it allows one to test that a pair of binary observables \emph{anticommutes}; both properties are used in the Pauli basis test.  \section{The classical low individual degree game}
 % Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
 \label{sec:ld-verifier}
 \label{sec:ld-game}
 
 The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	This note fixes terminology for a recurring failure mode in the formalization
    20	of the low individual degree test paper, \path{arXiv:2009.12982}.  It
    21	complements the note-writing policy in \path{docs/paper-gaps/policy.tex} and
    22	the source-statement audit tracked historically in \ghissue{1458}.  The current
    23	source-boundary proof holes are tracked in \ghissue{1507} and \ghissue{422}.
    24	A proof may be blocked at
    25	an intermediate mathematical assertion.  If that assertion is added as a new
    26	hypothesis to a theorem labelled as a paper theorem, the resulting \Lean{}
    27	theorem
    28	may be correct as a conditional statement, but it is no longer the theorem in
    29	the cited source.  The apparent proof has not closed the paper theorem; it has
    30	moved a proof obligation into the theorem statement.
    31	
    32	The protocol below distinguishes such proof debt from legitimate formal
    33	boundary conditions and from genuine mathematical corrections.  It is meant for
    34	contributors and reviewers who must decide whether a bridge, residual, repair,
    35	input, or obligation structure is a proved local construction, a tracked proof
    36	gap, or statement drift which must be repaired before a theorem may be
    37	advertised as a source theorem.  The default rule is restrictive: such data
    38	must not be added to a paper-facing theorem unless it is part of the cited
    39	source statement or a documented faithful encoding of its ambient hypotheses.
    40	
    41	\section{Basic objects}
    42	
    43	\paragraph{Source theorem.}
    44	A source theorem is a theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary in the paper
    45	source under \path{references/ldt-paper/}.  Its hypotheses and conclusion are
    46	the mathematical ground truth, subject only to faithful formal encoding and to
    47	documented paper-gap corrections.
    48	
    49	\paragraph{Paper-facing declaration.}
    50	A \Lean{} declaration is paper-facing when it is named or cited as the
    51	formalization of a source theorem, for instance through a blueprint
    52	\verb|\lean{}| link on a theorem environment carrying a paper label.  Such a
    53	declaration must match the source theorem in its public statement.  In
    54	particular, it may not add an unproved bridge, residual, repair, input,
    55	obligation structure, or other proof-obligation hypothesis which the paper does
    56	not assume.
    57	
    58	\paragraph{Proof obligation.}
    59	A proof obligation is an intermediate assertion needed by the proof of a source
    60	theorem.  It may be a construction, an estimate, a transport lemma, or a
    61	comparison between two formal representations.  If the paper proves or invokes
    62	this assertion, then the formalization should state it as a separate lemma or
    63	theorem and prove it from the upstream hypotheses.
    64	
    65	\paragraph{Obligation discharger.}
    66	An obligation discharger is a theorem or definition which constructs a proof
    67	obligation from the paper hypotheses already available at that point in the
    68	argument.  This is the preferred representation of missing work.  If the proof
    69	is not yet complete, the discharger may temporarily contain a tracked
    70	\verb|sorry|, but the paper-facing theorem should call it rather than assume
    71	its output as an additional theorem hypothesis.
    72	
    73	\paragraph{Conditional helper.}
    74	A conditional helper is a separately named theorem whose statement explicitly
    75	assumes a proof obligation.  Names such as
    76	\leanid{mainFormal\_ofInternalObligations},
    77	\leanid{orthonormalization\_ofInput}, or names whose suffix advertises the
    78	assumed obligation are permitted only when the declaration is not presented as
    79	the source theorem.  A conditional helper is a quarantine for downstream proof
    80	content; it does not close the source theorem.
    81	
    82	\section{Bridge, residual, repair, input, and obligation structures}
    83	
    84	The words \emph{bridge}, \emph{residual}, \emph{repair}, \emph{input}, and
    85	\emph{obligation structure} name possible formal shapes.  They become dangerous
    86	when their mathematical status is unclear or when their names make unproved
    87	data look like acceptable hypotheses of a source theorem.
    88	
    89	\paragraph{Bridge.}
    90	A bridge should be a transport theorem between two already defined
    91	mathematical forms: for example, a tensor-placement identity, a conversion
    92	between two equivalent consistency relations, or a statement translating a
    93	source object into a formal representation.  A bridge is harmless only after it
    94	is proved from previously available assumptions.  It becomes proof debt when it
    95	is assumed because the transport has not yet been proved.  It becomes theorem
    96	drift when the assumed bridge is added to a paper-facing theorem.
    97	
    98	\paragraph{Residual.}
    99	A residual is a named remainder after part of an argument has been performed.
   100	It is often a useful way to record the exact missing target after a completed
   101	construction.  A residual may appear as the conclusion of a helper theorem or
   102	as the input of a quarantined conditional helper.  It is not a permissible new
   103	assumption on a paper theorem unless the paper itself assumes that residual.
   104	
   105	\paragraph{Input.}
   106	An input is a named bundle of data or hypotheses consumed by a construction or
   107	conditional helper.  It is harmless only when each load-bearing field is either
   108	part of the source hypotheses or is produced by an earlier theorem.  It becomes
   109	proof debt when the bundle is merely assumed because the construction of its
   110	fields is missing.  It becomes theorem drift when such a bundle is added to the
   111	public statement of a source theorem.
   112	
   113	\paragraph{Repair.}
   114	A repair is a mathematical construction which replaces an approximate or
   115	partial object by a better object, usually with a quantitative estimate.  In
   116	the low individual degree test formalization, projectivization and
   117	orthonormalization repairs are genuine mathematical operations.  A repair
   118	should therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the
   119	corresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead
   120	of constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.
   121	
   122	\paragraph{Obligation structure.}
   123	An obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates
   124	needed by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target
   125	or as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement
   126	drift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed
   127	inside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is
   128	proved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing
   129	obligation.
   130	
   131	\section{The main failure mode}
   132	
   133	Suppose the paper proves
   134	\[
   135	  H \Longrightarrow C.
   136	\]
   137	During formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \(B\).  The
   138	paper theorem should be represented as
   139	\[
   140	  H \Longrightarrow B \Longrightarrow C
   141	  \quad\text{inside the proof,}
   142	\]
   143	where \(B\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \(H\).  The following
   144	public statement is a different theorem:
   145	\[
   146	  H \land B \Longrightarrow C.
   147	\]
   148	It is not unsound in \Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the
   149	conclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a
   150	conditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's
   151	conclusion.
   152	
   153	This is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge
   154	hypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted
   155	from the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide
   156	the hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a
   157	paper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a
   158	named internal proof obligation.
   159	
   160	\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}
   161	
   162	Not every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are
   163	faithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include
   164	nonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a
   165	quantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,
   166	or decidability instances required by \Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable
   167	when they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a
   168	condition used implicitly in the paper.
   169	
   170	The distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the
   171	domain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a
   172	mathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis
   173	leaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the
   174	hypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.
   175	
   176	\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}
   177	
   178	Definition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a
   179	definition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,
   180	then every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile
   181	while proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements
   182	can then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because
   183	the wrong definition is still upstream.
   184	
   185	When a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree
   186	protocol.
   187	
   188	\begin{enumerate}
   189	  \item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.
   190	  \item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem
   191	  relating the existing definition to the source object.
   192	  \item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.
   193	  \item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather
   194	  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.
   195	  \item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation
   196	  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.
   197	\end{enumerate}
   198	
   199	This is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local
   200	definition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.
   201	
   202	\section{Allowed shapes}
   203	
   204	\begin{center}
   205	\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\linewidth}p{0.31\linewidth}p{0.32\linewidth}}
   206	\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Allowed use} & \textbf{Forbidden use} \\
   207	\hline
   208	Paper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &
   209	Carries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or
   210	proof-obligation hypotheses \\
   211	Source-shaped theorem with a tracked \verb|sorry| & Default repair when the
   212	source proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened
   213	theorem statement merely to keep the file compiling \\
   214	Conditional helper & Temporary quarantine for substantial proof content whose
   215	remaining named obligation has not yet been discharged & Introduced merely to
   216	avoid a \verb|sorry|, or linked as the source theorem or marked as
   217	proof-complete for that theorem \\
   218	Obligation discharger theorem & Constructs the obligation from paper hypotheses &
   219	Merely restates the obligation as an assumption \\
   220	Input bundle & Collects produced data for a local construction & Is assumed by a
   221	source theorem instead of being produced \\
   222	Obligation structure & Bundles constructed data and estimates & Hides unproved
   223	fields that are then assumed by a source theorem \\
   224	Paper-gap note & Documents a real mathematical or formal-statement divergence &
   225	Justifies silent statement drift without a repair plan
   226	\end{tabular}
   227	\end{center}

   229	\section{Protocol for a blocked proof}
   230	
   231	When a source-labelled proof is blocked, use the following order.
   232	
   233	\begin{enumerate}
   234	  \item Read the cited source statement and the proof passage in
   235	  \path{references/ldt-paper/}.
   236	  \item Write the paper theorem form, the current \Lean{} theorem form, and the
   237	  first missing intermediate assertion.
   238	  \item Decide whether the missing assertion is a faithful boundary condition,
   239	  a representation adapter, an ordinary lemma from the paper proof, or a real
   240	  paper-gap discrepancy.
   241	  \item If it is an ordinary lemma or adapter, create a named theorem which
   242	  discharges that obligation.  Do not add it to the source theorem as a new
   243	  hypothesis.
   244	  \item Keep the source-labelled theorem itself in the source form, even if its
   245	  proof must contain a tracked \verb|sorry|.  This is the default repair when
   246	  the missing assertion has not yet been proved.
   247	  \item Create a conditional helper only to quarantine substantial proof content
   248	  that already exists and would otherwise be lost.  Do not create such a helper
   249	  merely to avoid a \verb|sorry| or to keep making progress.  If a conditional
   250	  helper remains, give it a conditional name, keep it separate from the
   251	  paper-facing theorem, and record the obligation discharger that must eliminate
   252	  it.
   253	  \item If the source and formal statements genuinely differ, write or update a
   254	  note under \path{docs/paper-gaps/} before marking the statement as aligned.
   255	  \item Update the blueprint so that paper labels point only to paper-facing
   256	  declarations.  Conditional helpers belong in remarks or implementation
   257	  notes, not in the source theorem block.
   258	\end{enumerate}
   259	
   260	\section{Retirement criterion}
   261	
   262	An auxiliary declaration should be removed from the main blueprint route, or
   263	renamed and documented as a purely internal lemma, when all three of the
   264	following conditions hold:
   265	\begin{enumerate}
   266	  \item it is not a statement in the cited paper and is not an explicitly cited
   267	        outside result;
   268	  \item no current proof of a paper-level target needs it as stated;
   269	  \item it assumes stronger proof data, finite-length data, completion data,
   270	        repair data, synchronization data, or package fields than the paper
   271	        proof requires.
   272	\end{enumerate}
   273	If such a declaration is still useful as a formal intermediate result, it
   274	should remain a lemma or a visibly conditional helper with a planned discharge.
   275	It should not be a headline replacement for the paper theorem, and it should
   276	not support a source-labelled blueprint \verb|\leanok| claim.
   277

    17	\section{Purpose}
    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,

   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in

   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if

HEAD:blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:164:	The two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\code^{\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, agrees with the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$ on every question pair whose diagonal-line direction is nonzero: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test.    102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   441		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset

   448		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis

   451		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   452		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).

   330	\begin{remark}[Norm conventions in the robustness bound]\label{rem:pauli-robustness-form}
   331		The proof above, following the source, establishes the first conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in the squared form $\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$, whereas the theorem bounds the unsquared norm by $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$.    332	\end{remark}

   132	\begin{definition}
   133	  \label{def:comm-strategy}
   134	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a game, and let
   135	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy for $\game$ such that  $\mH_A = \mH_B$.
   136	  Let $S \subseteq \cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$ denote the support of the question
   137	  distribution $\mu$, i.e.\ the set of $(x,y)$ such that $\mu(x,y)>0$.
   138	  We say that $\strategy$ is a \emph{commuting strategy for $\game$} if for all
   139	  question pairs $(x, y) \in S$, we have $[A^x_a, B^y_b] = 0$ 
   140	  for all $a
   141	  \in \cal{A}, b \in \cal{B}$, where $[A, B] = AB - BA$ denotes the commutator.
   142	\end{definition}

   144	\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]
   145	  \label{def:consistent-measurement}
   146	  Let $\cal{A}$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$ be a
   147	  state, and let $\{ M_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ be a projective measurement on
   148	  $\mH$.
   149	  We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if
   150	  and only if
   151	  \begin{equation*}
   152	    \forall a \in \mA\;,\quad M_a \otimes \Id_\bob\, \ket{\psi}
   153	    = \Id_\alice \otimes M_a\, \ket{\psi}\;.
   154	  \end{equation*}
   155		When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent}.
   156	\end{definition}
   157	
   158	The terminology ``consistent'' arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is 
   159	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} \,=\,1\;,\]
   160	where the first equality is by definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a=\Id$.

   162	\begin{definition}[Consistent strategies]
   163	  \label{def:consistent-strategy}
   164		Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a projective strategy with state
   165	  $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$, for some Hilbert space~$\mH$, which is

   167	  $\cal{A}$ and~$\cal{B}$, respectively.

   171	    \cal{B}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   172	\end{definition}
   173

   177	  \label{def:spcc}
   178	  We say that a strategy $\strategy$ for a game $\game$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\game$.
   179	  Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.
   180	\end{definition}

   183	Recall that for a (pure) state $\ket{\psi}\in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$, the \emph{Schmidt rank} of $\ket{\psi}$ is the smallest integer $k$ such that 
   184	\[ \ket{\psi} = \sum_{i=1}^k\, \alpha_i \ket{u_i}\otimes \ket{v_i}\;,\]

The coefficients $\alpha_i$ are uniquely defined by $\ket{\psi}$ and called \emph{Schmidt coefficients}.     22	\section{At a glance}
    23	
    24	\begin{itemize}
    25	  \item \textbf{Difficulty: easy.}  The issue is a quantifier exchange between
    26	  a supremum and an attained maximum in a preliminary lemma on nonlocal games.
    27	  No analytic estimate is missing; the substance is deciding which statement
    28	  the symmetrization proof supports and which statement the later arguments
    29	  consume.
    30	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight:} about \textbf{1--2 lemma interfaces} and on
    31	  the order of \textbf{100--300 lines} of formal proof for the value-preserving
    32	  symmetrization construction.  The attainment step itself should not be
    33	  formalized as printed (see the Conclusion).

    35	  (finite-dimensional inner product spaces, tensor products, block

    38	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs:} the completed projective form of

    44	\section{Key theorem forms}
    45	
    46	Three statements must be kept apart.  Throughout, $\game$ denotes a symmetric
    47	two-player one-round game and $\eps \ge 0$ a real parameter; the notation is
    48	introduced in the next section.
    49	
    50	\begin{enumerate}
    51	  \item \textbf{Source form (attainment form).}  If
    52	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and projective
    53	  strategy $\strategy$ with $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps$.
    54	  \item \textbf{Approximate form (what the source proof establishes).}  If
    55	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then for every $\eps' > \eps$ there exists a
    56	  symmetric and projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    57	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps'$.
    58	  \item \textbf{Given-strategy form (value-preserving symmetrization).}  If
    59	  $\strategy'$ is any strategy for $\game$ with
    60	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and
    61	  projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    62	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$.
    63	\end{enumerate}
    64	
    65	The source proof consists exactly of a proof of the third form, applied to a
    66	strategy supplied by the definition of the supremum; this yields the second
    67	form.  The first form asserts strictly more than the second, and the passage
    68	from the second to the first is the gap discussed in this note.  Every use of
    69	the lemma, in the source and in this project, consumes only the second or the
    70	third form.
    71	
    72	\section{The source assertion}
    73	
    74	A two-player one-round game
    75	$\game = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ in compact symmetric notation
    76	consists of a finite question alphabet $\mathcal X$, a finite answer alphabet
    77	$\mathcal A$, a symmetric question distribution $\mu$ on
    78	$\mathcal X \times \mathcal X$, and a decision predicate $D$ treating the two
    79	players symmetrically.  A tensor product strategy
    80	$\strategy = (\ket\psi, A, B)$ consists of a unit vector $\ket\psi$ in a
    81	tensor product $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ of \emph{finite-dimensional}
    82	Hilbert spaces together with POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ for the two
    83	players; its value $\val^*(\game, \strategy)$ is the acceptance probability,
    84	and the value of the game is the supremum
    85	\begin{equation*}
    86	  \val^*(\game) = \sup_{\strategy} \val^*(\game, \strategy)
    87	\end{equation*}
    88	over all tensor product strategies.  A strategy is projective if all its
    89	measurements are projective, and symmetric if the state is
    90	permutation-invariant on $\mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$ and both players use the
    91	same measurements.
    92	
    93	The symmetrization lemma of \cite[Section~5]{Ji2020MIPStar} asserts:%
    94	\footnote{The statement is at
    95	\path{references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex}, lines~94--99,
    96	and its proof at lines~101--132.  The blueprint statement restored to this form
    97	is \path{lem:symmetric-strat} in
    98	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex}.}
    99	if $\game$ is a symmetric game with $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some
   100	$\eps \ge 0$, then
   101	\begin{equation*}
   102	  \exists\, \strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M) \text{ symmetric and projective}
   103	  \quad\text{with}\quad
   104	  \val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps.
   105	  \tag{\path{lem:symmetric-strat}}
   106	\end{equation*}
   107	
   108	Its proof runs as follows.  For every $\eps' > \eps$ the definition of the
   109	supremum supplies a strategy $\strategy' = (\ket{\psi'}, A, B)$ with
   110	$\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps'$.  By Naimark dilation in the completed
   111	projective form of \cite[Theorem~5.1]{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} one may take
   112	$\ket{\psi'} \in \C^d_{A'} \ot \C^d_{B'}$ for some integer $d$ with all
   113	measurements projective.  One then forms the permutation-invariant state
   114	\begin{equation*}
   115	  \ket{\psi} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}
   116	  \bigl( \ket{0}_A \ket{1}_B \ket{\psi'}_{A'B'}
   117	       + \ket{1}_A \ket{0}_B \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{A'B'} \bigr)
   118	\end{equation*}
   119	on $(\C^2 \ot \C^d) \ot (\C^2 \ot \C^d)$, where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ permutes
   120	the two players' registers, and the block-diagonal projective measurements
   121	$M^x_a = \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \ot A^x_a + \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \ot B^x_a$.  Symmetry
   122	of $D$ gives $\val^*(\game, (\ket\psi, M)) = \val^*(\game, \strategy')$.  The
   123	construction is therefore \emph{value-preserving}: applied to any strategy it
   124	produces a symmetric projective strategy of exactly the same value.  What the
   125	proof establishes is thus the given-strategy form, hence the approximate form;
   126	the printed conclusion is the attainment form.
   127	
   128	\section{Why attainment does not follow}
   129	
   130	The supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ ranges over strategies on
   131	finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces of unbounded dimension.  The strategies
   132	$\strategy'_{\eps'}$ produced for $\eps' \downarrow \eps$ may require
   133	dimensions $d(\eps')$ growing without bound, and there is no compactness
   134	across dimensions from which a limiting finite-dimensional strategy of value
   135	at least $1-\eps$ could be extracted.  A symmetric projective strategy of
   136	value at least $1-\eps = \val^*(\game)$ would attain the supremum, so the
   137	printed conclusion is equivalent, under its hypothesis, to the assertion that
   138	$\val^*(\game)$ is attained by some strategy.  No general principle supplies
   139	this: it is known, and recalled in the introduction of the source itself, that
   140	the set of finite-dimensional quantum correlations is not closed and differs
   141	from the set of infinite-dimensional spatial correlations, so limits of
   142	finite-dimensional strategies need not be realized by any finite-dimensional
   143	strategy.  Whether some symmetric game realizes the failure --- a game whose
   144	value is attained by no tensor product strategy, presented together with the
   145	exposing functional as a decision predicate --- is a separate question that
   146	this note does not need to settle.  The local verdict is about the proof: the
   147	cited argument proves the approximate form and does not prove the attainment
   148	form.
   149	
   150	\section{Uses of the lemma}
   151	
   152	The source invokes the lemma twice.
   153	
   154	First, in the soundness proof for the oracularization transformation, the
   155	argument fixes a strategy $\strategy^{\mathrm{orac}}$ for the oracularized game
   156	``with value $1-\eps$'' and applies the lemma to assume without loss of
   157	generality that it is projective.%
   158	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/10_oracularization.tex},
   159	lines~317--321.}
   160	Here the input is a given strategy, not the value of the game; the
   161	given-strategy form applies verbatim and preserves the value exactly, so the
   162	use is justified by what the proof establishes.
   163	
   164	Second, in the soundness proof for answer reduction, the argument assumes the
   165	strict inequality $\val^*(\game) > 1-\eps$ and concludes that there is a
   166	symmetric projective strategy of value greater than $1-\eps$.%
   167	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/11_answer_reduction.tex},
   168	lines~2322--2332.}
   169	Writing $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps_0$ with $\eps_0 < \eps$ and applying the
   170	approximate form with $\eps' = (\eps+\eps_0)/2$ produces a symmetric
   171	projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps' > 1-\eps$.  A strict lower
   172	bound on the supremum thus passes through the approximate form; attainment is
   173	not used.
   174	
   175	In this project, the soundness statements of the Pauli basis test track
   176	quantify over strategies assumed to succeed with probability at least
   177	$1-\eps$, so any symmetrization step starts from a given strategy and consumes
   178	the given-strategy form.  The blueprint currently records the lemma as part of
   179	the games vocabulary and has no downstream dependency on it; the two source
   180	uses above belong to transformations outside the scope of the present
   181	development.  Consequently, no consumer of the lemma --- in the source or here
   182	--- requires the attainment form.
   183	
   184	\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
   185	
   186	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} states the lemma in the source shape.
   187	Its proof records the value-preserving construction and the approximate form
   188	that the construction yields, and explicitly marks the remaining attainment
   189	step as unproved, citing this note; an accompanying remark summarizes the
   190	obstruction.  An earlier revision of the blueprint had instead weakened the
   191	source-labelled conclusion to the approximate form; following the project's
   192	proof-gap protocol, the source-labelled statement is restored and the missing
   193	step is tracked in the proof rather than absorbed into the statement.  No
   194	\Lean{} declaration is currently linked to the lemma.
   195	
   196	\section{Conclusion}
   197	
   198	The verdict is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma: the symmetrization
   199	argument proves the given-strategy and approximate forms, while the printed
   200	conclusion additionally asserts that the supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ is
   201	attained, which does not follow.  The gap is harmless for the results built on
   202	the lemma, since both uses in the source, and all planned uses in this
   203	project, proceed from a given strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ or from a
   204	strict lower bound on the value, for which the value-preserving construction
   205	suffices.  For stage~4 (formalization) the recommendation is: formalize the
   206	given-strategy symmetrization lemma as the workhorse statement; keep the
   207	source-labelled lemma in source shape with the attainment step an explicit,
   208	tracked proof obligation; and do not strengthen the source-labelled statement's
   209	hypotheses or weaken its conclusion silently.  If a later investigation
   210	settles the counterexample question for symmetric games, the statement should
   211	then be reclassified from an unproved step to a documented statement
   212	correction.

   175	We recall the Magic Square game of Mermin and Peres. It is a simple self-test for two EPR pairs, and it allows one to test that a pair of binary observables \emph{anticommutes}; both properties are used in the Pauli basis test. Here it is presented as a binary constraint satisfaction game.    180

   183			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} &= \{\mathsf{Constraint}_i : i = 1,2,\ldots,6\}\;,\\
   184			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}} &= \{\mathsf{Variable}_j : j = 1,2,\ldots,9\}\;,\\
   185			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} &= \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} \cup \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}\;,
   186		\end{align*}
   187		where $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ denotes the constraint of row $i$ (with variables $x_{3(i-1)+1}, x_{3(i-1)+2}, x_{3(i-1)+3}$), $\mathsf{Constraint}_4$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_5$ denote the constraints of the first two columns, and $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$ denotes the constraint of the third column (with variables $x_{i-3}, x_{i}, x_{i+3}$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$, $i \in \{4,5,6\}$).

    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
