   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.

   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or

   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.

+\section{At a glance}

+\begin{itemize}

+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple of the Pauli basis
+test, $\ket{\hat\psi}$ is the expanded state of the projective strategy
+under analysis, succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, and all
+approximations are with respect to $\ket{\hat\psi}$.  For lines
+$\ell_X, \ell_Z$ in $\F_q^m$, the POVM $\{T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\}$,
+with outcomes pairs of polynomials of degree at most $md$ on the two
+lines, is the two-basis combined line measurement, and
+$\{\hat Q^{x,z}_{a,b}\}$ is the combined point measurement; their
+consistency errors are $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$ and
+$\delta_Q = \poly(\eps)$ respectively, and
+$\delta_{\mathrm{Line}} = \poly(\eps)$ is the line--point consistency
+error of the strategy.  The lemma under discussion asserts that a
+measurement $\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, built for each line $\ell$ in
+$\F_q^{2m+2}$, is $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$-consistent, on average over
+the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$, with the combined point
+measurement on the extended coordinates, together with the
+register-swapped counterpart.%
+\footnote{In the mirror of the source consulted here,

+\section{The source assertion and the two routes}
+
+The source proof in \cite{Ji2020MIPStar} constructs $\hat Q^{\ell}_f$ by
+averaging, over a distribution $D$ on tuples $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$
+provided by its sub-line lemma, the pushforward of
+$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}$ along a combining map, and reduces the lemma to a
+bound on the scalar consistency defect
+\begin{equation}
+  \Lambda \,=\,
+  \E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
+  \E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
+  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
+  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
+  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
+  \ket{\hat\psi}\,,
+  \tag{\path{eq:qld-combined-lines-consistency}}
+\end{equation}
+in which the point $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ is uniform on $\ell$ and the sum
+ranges over pairs of line polynomials.  The proof then bounds $\Lambda$
+twice, by different routes and with different results, and the printed
+record is internally inconsistent: the display introducing $\Lambda$
+asserts the first-route bound, while the closing lines assert the
+second-route bound as the operative one; the lemma statement claims a
+third form matching neither.
+
+\paragraph{The first route.}
+Three claims are chained.  The combined point measurement
+$\hat Q^{x,z}$ is replaced by the ordered product of the two point
+measurements at cost $\delta_Q^{1/2}$; the $X$-point factor is removed at
+cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$; and the remaining $Z$-point
+correlation is shown to be within
+$\sqrt{m}\,(\delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4} + \eps^{1/4})$ of one.  The
+factors of $m$ enter through the mixture structure of the sub-line
+distribution: each restricted line distribution carries mixture weight
+$1/(2m)$ in the line-point distribution, so an average bounded by
+$\delta$ over the full distribution is bounded only by $2m\delta$ over a
+restricted component and by $4m^2\delta$ over a product of two
+components, and the Cauchy--Schwarz steps halve the exponents.  Chaining
+the claims gives
+\begin{equation*}
+  \Lambda \,=\, O\big(m\,(\eps^{1/4} + \delta_P^{1/4} + \delta_Q^{1/4}
+  + \delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2})\big)
+  \,=\, m \cdot \poly(\eps,\, md/q)\,.
+\end{equation*}
+One intermediate assertion needs a harmless correction: the final line
+of the proof of the second claim asserts the bound
+$O(m^2 \delta_{\mathrm{Line}})$ for a consistency term that is close to
+one, rather than for its deficit.  Read as a bound on the deficit ---
+which is what the surrounding Cauchy--Schwarz argument requires and what
+the invoked line--point consistency provides after the mixture
+inflation --- the claim and its use are correct, with the square root of
+the deficit giving the stated cost $m\,\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}^{1/2}$.
+
+\paragraph{The second route.}
+After the chain, the source restarts: it asserts that, by Property~2 of
+its sub-line lemma, $\Lambda$ is a mixture, over types
+$\mathrm{v}_1, \mathrm{v}_2 \in \{\mathrm{ALine}, \mathrm{DLine}\}$ and
+indices $i, j \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, of terms
+\begin{equation*}
+  \E_{(\ell_X, x) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_1,i}}\
+  \E_{(\ell_Z, z) \sim D_{\mathrm{v}_2,j}}
+  \sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
+  \big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
+  \big(\Id - \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
+  \ket{\hat\psi}
+\end{equation*}
+over two \emph{independently} sampled restricted line-point pairs,
+bounds each term by $O(m^2\delta_P)$ using the restricted-distribution
+consequence of the two-basis line lemma, and concludes
+$\Lambda = O(m^2\delta_P)$.  The invoked decomposition concerns the
+\emph{joint} law of the pair $((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z))$, where $x$ and
+$z$ are the two blocks of the single point sampled on $\ell$.  Property~2
+of the sub-line lemma does not assert this joint law: it asserts the
+component-wise product law of the pair of \emph{lines}
+$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, and the conditional uniformity of each point on its
+line separately --- equivalently, the laws of the two pairs
+$((\ell_X, x), (\ell_Z, z'))$ and $((\ell_X, x'), (\ell_Z, z))$ in which
+the \emph{other} point is resampled independently.  These marginal
+statements are exactly what the first route's claims consume, each
+involving one point at a time; the joint decomposition used by the
+second route is a strictly stronger property and is not established by
+the lemma it is attributed to.
+
+\section{Why neither route yields the stated form}
+
+The stated error form is $\poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$, a function of the two
+quantities $m^2\eps$ and $md/q$ that vanishes as both vanish.  The
+first-route bound is not dominated by any such function: along the
+scaling $\eps = m^{-4}$ with $q/(md) \to \infty$, both $m^2\eps = m^{-2}$
+and $md/q$ tend to $0$, while the term $m\,\eps^{1/4} = 1$ does not.
+Hence the established derivation supports no bound of the claimed form.
+The second-route bound, even granting the missing decomposition, carries
+the separate prefactor $m^2$: writing $\delta_P = \poly(\eps, md/q)$
+with some fixed positive exponents, the contribution
+$m^2 (md/q)^{c}$ is not dominated by any vanishing function of $m^2\eps$
+and $md/q$, as the scaling $\eps = 0$, $md/q = m^{-2/c}$ shows, and the
+$\eps$-contribution fails similarly for sublinear exponents.  Neither
+observation asserts that the \emph{conclusion} of the lemma is false for
+some error function of the claimed form; the defect is that the printed
+proof does not deliver it.
+
+For orientation, the algebraic identity
+$m\,\eps^{1/2} = (m^2\eps)^{1/2}$ shows what a derivation of the claimed
+$\eps$-dependence would need: a chain that loses only square roots in the
+$\eps$-type quantities \emph{after} the restricted-distribution
+inflation would produce terms of the shape $(m^2\eps)^{1/2}$.  The
+printed chain loses fourth roots, through two nested Cauchy--Schwarz
+steps applied to already square-rooted quantities, and its
+$md/q$-dependence enters as $m\,\delta_P^{1/4}$, which the claimed form
+cannot absorb.
+
+\section{Candidate repairs}
+
+The following are candidate directions, with their open obligations; none
+of the routes below is claimed as established.
+

+Adopt $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}} = m \cdot \poly(\eps, md/q)$ ---
+concretely, the first-route bound --- as the operative error form.  Open
+obligations: (i)~verify that every consumer tolerates the prefactor; in
+the source and in the blueprint the only consumer is the polynomial-pair
+lemma, whose imported error
+$a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ absorbs

   101	\section{Consistency with the points measurements}
   102	
   103	The next lemma shows that the pulled-apart measurements are consistent with the original points measurements of the strategy, and self-consistent. In its statement, and for the remainder of the chapter, $\delta_S$ denotes the function of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, enlarged by an adjustment of the universal constants $a$ and $b$ so as to also dominate additional error terms of order $\sqrt{\eps}$, $\eps$, and $md/q$ that the source absorbs into $\delta_S$ along the way; such an adjustment is possible since, after shrinking $b$ to at most $1/2$, the term $\eps^b$ dominates $\sqrt{\eps}$ and $\eps$ for $\eps \leq 1$, while $(md)^a q^{-b}$ dominates $md/q$.
   104	
   105	\begin{lemma}[Consistency and self-consistency of the pulled-apart measurements]\label{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}
   106		\uses{def:tilde-m-measurement, def:tilde-w-observables, def:projective-strategy-setup, def:expanded-state, def:consistency, def:povm-distance, lem:qld-4-7, def:indicator-vector}
   107		The measurements $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ and observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ satisfy the following properties.
   108		% The paper's statement also quantifies item 1 over j, but j does not occur
   109		% in item 1; the vacuous quantifier is dropped here.
   110		\begin{enumerate}
   111			\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over uniformly random $u \in \F_q^m$,
   112			\[
   113				\Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \simeq_{\delta_S} M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''}
   114			\]
   115			and
   116			\[
   117				\tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \ot \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''} \simeq_{\delta_S} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \ot M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\;,
   118			\]
   119			with the answer summation over $a \in \F_q$.
   120			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, on average over uniformly random $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{M}$,
   121			\[
   122				\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ot \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''} \approx_{\delta_S} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \ot \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})\;.
   123			\]
   124		\end{enumerate}
   125	\end{lemma}
   245	\begin{lemma}[Extraction of the EPR state and the Pauli observables]\label{lem:qld-unitary}
   246		\uses{lem:qld-4-7, def:v-swap-unitary, def:expanded-state, def:projective-strategy-setup, def:generalized-pauli, def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
   247		There exists a function $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$, where $\delta_S$ is the function of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, and there exist unitaries $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ acting on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ and $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ acting on registers $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, such that the following hold.
   248		\begin{enumerate}
   249			\item There exists a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$ such that
   250			\[
   251				\bigl\| V_{\mathrm{A}} \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\hat{\psi}}_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}}_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \bigr\|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}\;.
   252			\]
   253			\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
   254			\begin{align*}
   255				V_{\mathrm{A}} \, \bigl(M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h \bigr)_{\mathrm{A}} \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''}\;, \\
   256				V_{\mathrm{B}} \, \bigl(M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h \bigr)_{\mathrm{B}} \, V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   257			\end{align*}
   258			where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''}$, with the answer summation over $h \in \F_q^{M}$ and no average over questions.
   259		\end{enumerate}
   260		The unitaries may be taken to be $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:v-swap-unitary}.
   261	\end{lemma}
   262	\begin{proof}
   263		\uses{def:v-swap-unitary, lem:v-swap-conjugation, lem:tildew-product-form, lem:qld-construct-the-paulis, lem:qld-win-implications, fact:triangle-for-simeq, def:bracket, lem:cancellation, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree, lem:qld-4-7}
   264		For the first item, the self-consistency of the observables $\tilde{W}^j$ (Item~2 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}) is equivalent, since these observables are Hermitian involutions (Lemma~\ref{lem:tildew-product-form}), to $\E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M} \bra{\hat\psi} \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ot \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ket{\hat\psi} \geq 1 - \delta_S/2$; setting $\ket{\vartheta} = V_{\mathrm{A}} \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\hat\psi}$ and using the exact conjugation identities of Lemma~\ref{lem:v-swap-conjugation}, this becomes $\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - \delta_S/2$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$, where $H_W = \E_j \E_{\tilde{u}} \, \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \ot \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = \bigl( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(s) \ot \tau^W(s) \bigr)^{\ot M}$ by the tensor factorization of $\tau^W(\tilde{u})$ and the invariance of the uniform average over $s$ under $s \mapsto e_j s$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}, $\E_{s,s'} \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \ot \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ on each pair of qudits, whence $H_X H_Z = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$. The bounds $\| (\Id - H_W)\ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \leq \delta_S$ and $\bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - 2\delta_S$, combined through the triangle inequality $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \| \leq 2\sqrt{\delta_S}$ (see Remark~\ref{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}), give $\bra{\vartheta} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - 4\delta_S$.
   265		% Case distinction added: the source normalizes the projected vector
   266		% without ensuring that it is nonzero; see Remark rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip.
   267		If $\delta_S > 1/8$, then, after enlarging the universal constant in $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$, both items of the lemma hold with $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$ an arbitrary unit state, since their left-hand sides never exceed $4$; assume therefore $\delta_S \leq 1/8$. Then the vector $(\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta}$ has squared norm at least $1 - 4\delta_S \geq 1/2 > 0$, and $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$ may be defined as its normalization; the overlap of $\ket{\vartheta}$ with $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$ equals the norm of that vector and is at least $\sqrt{1 - 4\delta_S} \geq 1 - 4\delta_S$, which yields the first item with a bound of $8\delta_S = O(\sqrt{\delta_S})$. For the second item, Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications} gives, on average over $u \in \F_q^m$, $M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \ot \Id \simeq_\eps \Id \ot M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ and $\Id \ot M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \simeq_\eps M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \Id$, where $M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} = \sum_{h : g_h(u) = a} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h$; combining these with Item~1 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} by Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle-for-simeq}, using $\delta_S \geq \eps$, yields $M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \ot \Id \simeq_{\sqrt{\delta_S}} \Id \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a$. Writing $\ket{\Delta} = \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, the quantity to be bounded for the $\mathrm{A}$-side relation equals $2 - 2\sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_{\mathrm{A}} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \ot (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\Delta}$, since $(\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''} \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} = (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$. Replacing $(\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}$ by the averaged coarse-graining $\E_u \sum_{h' : g_{h'}(u) = g_h(u)} (\tau^W_{h'})_{\mathrm{B}''}$ costs at most $md/q$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} (distinct $h \neq h'$ have distinct encodings $g_h \neq g_{h'}$, of total degree at most $md$), and by \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the resulting sum equals $\E_u \sum_{a} \bra{\Delta} V_{\mathrm{A}} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger \ket{\Delta}$. Exchanging $\ket{\Delta}$ for $\ket{\vartheta}$ costs $O(\delta_S^{1/4})$ by the first item, and the resulting expression $\E_u \sum_a \bra{\hat\psi} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \ket{\hat\psi}$ is at least $1 - O(\sqrt{\delta_S})$ by the $\simeq_{\sqrt{\delta_S}}$ relation above. Altogether the distance is $O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$; the $\mathrm{B}$-side relation is proved identically.
   268	\end{proof}

   270	\begin{remark}[Two steps in the source proof of the extraction lemma]\label{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}
   271		In the source proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary}, the triangle inequality gives $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \| \leq \| (\Id - H_X)\ket{\vartheta} \| + \| (\Id - H_Z)\ket{\vartheta} \| \leq 2\sqrt{\delta_S}$, so that $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \leq 4\delta_S$; the source instead asserts the bound $2\sqrt{\delta_S}$ for the \emph{squared} norm, which holds only when $\sqrt{\delta_S} \leq 1/2$, and consequently carries the term $\sqrt{\delta_S}$ into an overlap bound of $1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S}$. The proof above uses the corrected bound $4\delta_S$, which gives the overlap bound $1 - 4\delta_S$ and leaves the final bound $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}} = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ unchanged. The source proof also normalizes the vector $(\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta}$ without ensuring that it is nonzero; the case distinction on $\delta_S$ in the proof above supplies this, the conclusions of the lemma being trivial when $\delta_S$ exceeds a universal constant.
   272	\end{remark}

Complements\\nthe lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference, which covers the kernel-level\\nblockers; this file covers patterns where the Lean code *compiles and the\\ntrick is at the level of what the statement says or what the definitions\\nbake in*.\\n\\nEvery pattern here is **castle-in-the-air in spirit**: a theorem named after a\\npaper result that doesn't actually prove it. The named offenders below all\\ncross-reference a concrete issue or PR so reviewers can see a real example.\\n\\n## Why this matters\\n\\nKernel checks are necessary but not sufficient. A theorem can:\\n\\n- Be marked `\\\\leanok` in the blueprint,\\n- Have a sorry-free proof body,\\n- Have a clean axiom closure (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` only),\\n\\nand still prove **nothing that the paper actually claims**, if the proof\\nobligation has been displaced into a hypothesis, a definition, or a sentinel\\nbranch. The patterns below are the displacement mechanisms we've seen in this\\ncodebase.\\n\\n## Catalogue\\n\\n- [A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis](#a1--conclusion-shaped-hypothesis)\\n- [A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand](#a2--definitional-sleight-of-hand)\\n- [A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions](#a3--zero-fallback-branches-hiding-preconditions)\\n- [A4 — Trivial default witnesses for existentials](#a4--trivial-default-witnesses-for-existentials)\\n- [A5 — Castle-in-the-air / bypassing Mathlib](#a5--castle-in-the-air--bypassing-mathlib)\\n- [A6 — External `*Statement` smuggles](#a6--external-statement-smuggles)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## A1 — Conclusion-shaped hypothesis\\n\\n**Smell.** The theorem takes a hypothesis whose type is the theorem's own\\nconclusion (or an `∃`/function that produces the conclusion). The proof body\\nis a trivial `rcases`/`exact`/`.trans`/`simpa using h` and does no\\nmathematical work. A variant wraps the hypothesis in a named bundle\\n(`*BridgePackage`, `*Statement`); see issues [#449], [#451], [#477] for the\\ncatalogue, and [#493] for the inline-existential mutation triggered by\\nPR [#491].\\n\\n### Why it's bad\\n\\nThe theorem's named mathematical content is never derived from prior lemmas;\\nthe caller (who supplies the hypothesis) has to discharge it. In practice the\\ncaller then has the same problem, pushing the obligation further up the\\nstack. The theorem is true under a vacuous hypothesis and the `\\\\leanok` tag\\nmisrepresents the actual state of the proof.\\n\\n### How to spot it\\n\\n- The hypothesis type contains, up to `∃` / `∧` / a coercion, the theorem's\\n  conclusion.\\n- The proof body is one of:\\n  - `rcases h with ⟨...⟩; exact ⟨...⟩`\\n  - `exact h.fieldName` / `exact h.a.trans h.b`\\n  - `by simpa using h.fieldName`\\n- The hypothesis is a bundle named `*BridgePackage`, `*Witness`, `*Package`,\\n  `*Output`, with a field whose type matches the conclusion structure.\\n- Consumers of the bundle are trivial (field projection + return).\\n\\n### Concrete example\\n\\nHistorical example (before the MainInductionStep cleanup):\\n\\n```lean\\ntheorem mainInduction\\n    (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q]\\n    (strategy : SymStrat params ι)\\n    (eps delta gamma : Error) (k : ℕ)\\n    (hbridge : MainInductionBridgePackage params strategy eps delta gamma k) :\\n    ∃ G : Measurement (Polynomial params) ι,\\n      ConsRel strategy.state ...\\n        (mainInductionError params k eps delta gamma) := by\\n  rcases hbridge.witness with ⟨error, G, hG, herror⟩\\n  refine ⟨G, ?_⟩\\n  exact ⟨le_trans hG.offDiagonalBound herror⟩\\n```\\n\\nHere `MainInductionBridgePackage.witness` has type\\n`∃ error, ∃ G, ConsRel ... error ∧ error ≤ mainInductionError ...` — literally\\nthe conclusion. The code has since been refactored to remove both this\\nspecific MainInductionStep bridge and the interim theorem alias that exposed\\nthe same witness shape under the paper theorem's name, but the snippet remains\\nthe archetypal example of the anti-pattern.\\n\\nPR [#491] proposed to delete the `*BridgePackage` by **inlining** the bundle's\\nfields as explicit hypotheses. That only scatters the same pattern across\\nindividual signatures without producing any proof — it's strictly worse\\nbecause the named bundle at least shows up in one tracker. Do not accept PRs\\nthat discharge an ungrounded bridge by flattening it into conclusion-shaped\\nexistential hypotheses, or by reintroducing the same shape under a theorem name\\nthat suggests the paper result has been proved.\\n\\n### How to fix it\\n\\nPrefer **proving a real intermediate lemma** — one that the paper also uses\\n— and stating its signature with the paper's hypotheses (not the theorem's\\nconclusion). Then use it inside the larger theorem. If the missing content\\ncannot be formalized yet, state the missing assertion as a named obligation\\nto be proved from the paper hypotheses, and leave the corresponding proof open\\nunder a tracker. Do not put that obligation on the source-labelled theorem as\\nan extra hypothesis. Existing `BridgePackage`-style declarations are proof\\ndebt to be removed or converted into source-faithful obligations; they are not\\nthe preferred shape for new work.\\n\\nA signature passes the smell test if:\\n\\n- Every hypothesis is a **named intermediate fact** that also appears in the\\n  paper or blueprint proof, not the theorem's output packaged up, and\\n- Replacing a hypothesis with its negation would produce a *different*\\n  theorem, not a trivially-false one.\\n\\n### Related issues and patterns\\n\\n- [#449] — paper-wide gap tracker\\n- [#451] — the tracked `BridgePackage` producer catalogue\\n- [#595] — resolved the QXP `ProjectiveNonMeasurementBridgePackage` offender by\\n  deleting the bridge and threading `RoundingToProjectorsWitness` directly\\n- [#477] — resolved `QXPLayerData` axiom-field projection (a definitional variant)\\n- [#493] — the inline-existential mutation of this pattern\\n- [#491] — PR that introduced the mutation\\n\\n---\\n\\n## A2 — Definitional sleight-of-hand\\n\\n**Smell.** A `def`/`abbrev` is written so its body is the paper's claim, and\\na nearby `theorem` restates that claim and proves it by `rfl` (or a one-line\\n`simp [foo]` where `foo` is the defining equation). The \\\"mathematical\\ncontent\\\" has been baked into the definition; the theorem is a tautology. See\\nissues [#477], [#494].\\n\\n### Why it's bad\\n\\n`rfl` proves that a definition equals itself. If the definition is chosen\\n*so that* it equals the conclusion, the `rfl` \\\"proof\\\" transports none of the\\npaper's reasoning — it is literally the reflexivity of a shape we invented to\\nmatch the conclusion. The real identity the paper proves (e.g.,\\n`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ` over an actual inner product) is still not stated\\nanywhere in Lean.\\n\\n### How to spot it\\n\\n- A `theorem` whose body is `rfl` / `by rfl` / `by simp [defName]` where\\n  `defName` is the def that unfolds to the conclusion.\\n- A `structure` with a `Prop`-typed field whose *role* in the paper is a\\n  nontrivial identity (SVD, orthonormality, Cauchy–Schwarz), accompanied by a\\n  constructor that discharges that field with `rfl`.\\n- A `def foo := if α = β then 1 else 0` followed by a theorem asserting\\n  `foo α β = if α = β then 1 else 0`.\\n- Bridge-like structures where every field is itself a function\\n  `(precondition) → (conclusion-step)` and the consumer applies the field\\n  directly.\\n\\n### Concrete example\\n\\nFrom `MIPStarRE/LDT/ExpansionHypercubeGraph/Defs/Fourier.lean`:\\n\\n```lean\\n/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/\\ndef fourierBasisInnerProduct (params : Parameters)\\n    (α β : Point params) : Error :=\\n  if α = β then 1 else 0\\n\\n/-- The exact inner-product formula for the hypercube Fourier basis. -/\\nlemma fourierBasisInnerProduct_eq (params : Parameters)\\n    (α β : Point params) :\\n    fourierBasisInnerProduct params α β = if α = β then 1 else 0 := rfl\\n\\n/-- `prop:eigenvectors`. -/\\ntheorem eigenvectors (params : Parameters) :\\n    (∀ α β : Point params,\\n      fourierBasisInnerProduct params α β = if α = β then 1 else 0) ∧ ... := by\\n  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩\\n  · intro α β\\n    exact fourierBasisInnerProduct_eq params α β    -- castle: def IS Kronecker delta\\n  ...\\n```\\n\\nThe paper's orthonormality claim — that the additive characters `φ_α` form an\\northonormal basis under the actual inner product\\n`⟨f, g⟩ := (1/|V|) · ∑_u f(u)^* · g(u)` — requires a genuine character-sum\\nidentity. The Lean theorem states and proves only the trivial fact that the\\ndefinition equals itself.\\n\\n### Not every `rfl` is a castle\\n\\nDistinguish from legitimate bookkeeping where a named equation is literally\\nhow something was defined. Example: `mainFormalError_eq_envelope` in\\n`Test/ErrorCascade/Definitions.lean` unfolds the definition of\\n`mainFormalError` to its envelope factorization. The mathematical content is\\nelsewhere (the envelope is derived from per-step bounds); the `rfl` theorem is\\na naming convenience only. The test is: **does the `def` body encode a paper\\nidentity, or does it just name a compound expression?**\\n\\n### How to fix it\\n\\n1. Move the paper's real definition to the concrete one: for Fourier, define\\n   the inner product as the actual sum over vertices, and the characters\\n   `φ_α` as functions from `Point params` to `ℂ`.\\n2. State the paper's identity (`⟨φ_α, φ_β⟩ = δ_αβ`) as a theorem over those\\n   concrete objects.\\n3. Prove it via the standard character-sum derivation (or cite the Mathlib\\n   counterpart if one exists — `Matrix.dotProduct` / `Finset.sum_eq_zero_iff`\\n   combined with `ZMod.sum_pow_units` style lemmas).\\n4. If you want to keep the Kronecker shorthand, define it *afterward* as a\\n   consequence, not as the primitive.\\n\\n### Related issues\\n\\n- [#477] — resolved `QXPLayerData` field projections (Ch4 SVD as axiom fields)\\n- [#494] — the Fourier case and other candidates\\n\\n---\\n\\n## A3 — Zero-fallback branches hiding preconditions\\n\\n**Smell.** A total function is defined by `if eligible then real_value else\\ndefault`, where the `default` (usually `0`, `default`, `⊥`, or\\n`Classical.arbitrary`) is a sentinel for \\\"precondition not met.\\\" Downstream\\ntheorems state properties that are only true on the eligible branch, but the\\ntheorem's type signature does not carry the eligibility proof, so the\\nobligation moves silently from the prover to whoever happens to call the\\nfunction. See issue [#495], related to [#307].\\n\\n### Why it's bad\\n\\nThe signature lies about the domain of validity. A caller passing a\\nnon-eligible input gets `0` back; any theorem proved about \\\"the output\\\" is\\nproved for `0`, which is trivially true and carries no information. When a\\nlater theorem composes the output with another lemma, the composition\\ntype-checks but the conclusion is vacuous on inputs where the original\\nprecondition failed.\\n\\nThe paper, by contrast, restricts the quantifier in the first place:\\n\\\"Fix a tuple `(x₁, ..., x_k)` with Hamming weight `≥ d+1`.\\\" The Lean should\\nmatch.\\n\\n### How to spot it\\n\\n- `match ... with | some _ => real | none => 0` or `| _ => 0`.\\n- `if hEligible : P then ... else default`.\\n- Identifier names containing `fallback`, `placeholder`, `sentinel`,\\n  `dummy`, `or0`, `orDefault`.\\n- Recursive definitions whose base case unconditionally returns a sentinel.\\n- Functions that return `Polynomial params` but can return the zero polynomial\\n  on inputs that shouldn't be in the domain.\\n\\n### Concrete example (historical; resolved by PR #561)\\n\\nUntil PR #561, `MIPStarRE/LDT/Pasting/Defs/Interpolation.lean` contained:\\n\\n```lean\\n/-- Extract the polynomial from a completed slice outcome; returns 0 on ⊥. -/\\nnoncomputable def extractSliceOr0 {params : Parameters} [FieldModel params.q]\\n    (g : GHatOutcome params) : PolynomialModel params :=\\n  match g with\\n  | some p => p.poly\\n  | none   => 0\\n```\\n\\nThe consumer `interpolateCompletedSlicesFromSupport` ran Lagrange\\ninterpolation on `extractSliceOr0`-extracted values. If the support contained\\na `none`, the interpolant silently pretended that slice evaluated to zero.\\nThe paper's Lagrange step is quantified over *eligible* slices only, so the\\nLean API should carry `∀ i ∈ support, (g i).isSome` as a hypothesis; instead\\nit carried nothing, and the theorem technically type-checked on inputs for\\nwhich its conclusion was meaningless.\\n\\n**Current status:** resolved. The live API now removes `extractSliceOr0`,\\nthreads the explicit hypothesis `hσsupport : σ ⊆ gHatTupleSupport gs` into\\n`interpolateCompletedSlicesFromSupport`, and packages the chosen support For the converse items, write the off-diagonal mass $\\sum_{a \\ne b} \\bra{\\psi} A^x_a \\ot B^x_b \\ket{\\psi}$ as an inner product involving $(A^x_a \\ot \\Id - \\Id \\ot B^x_a)\\ket{\\psi}$ and use projectivity of both families, or of one family combined with the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality; the latter route costs a square root in the error.\n   227\t\\end{proof}\n   228\t\n   229\t\\begin{lemma}[Fact 4.20 in \\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\\label{fact:add-a-proj}\n   230\t\t\\uses{def:povm-distance}\n   231\t\tLet $\\mathcal A, \\mathcal B, \\mathcal C$ be finite sets, and let $\\mu$ be a distribution over question pairs $(x,y)$. Then\n   235\t\t\\begin{align*}\n   236\t\t\t\\sum_c \\bigl\\lVert (C^y_{a,\\,c} A^x_{a,\\,b} - C^y_{a,\\,c} B^x_{a,\\,b})\\, \\ket{\\psi} \\bigr\\rVert^2\n   237\t\t\t&= \\bra{\\psi} (A^x_{a,\\,b} - B^x_{a,\\,b})^\\dagger \\Bigl( \\sum_c (C^y_{a,\\,c})^\\dagger C^y_{a,\\,c} \\Bigr) (A^x_{a,\\,b} - B^x_{a,\\,b}) \\ket{\\psi}\\\\\n   238\t\t\t&\\le \\bigl\\lVert (A^x_{a,\\,b} - B^x_{a,\\,b})\\, \\ket{\\psi} \\bigr\\rVert^2\\,,\n   239\t\t\\end{align*}\n   240\t\twhere the inequality uses the assumption $\\sum_c (C^y_{a,\\,c})^\\dagger C^y_{a,\\,c} \\le \\Id$. All expectations are taken according to $\\mu$, and the last quantity is at most $\\delta$ by assumption.\n   271\t\\end{proof}\n   272\t\n   273\t\\begin{lemma}[Triangle inequality; Fact 4.28 in \\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\\label{fact:triangle}\n   274\t\t\\uses{def:povm-distance}\n   275\t\tIf $A^x_a \\approx_\\delta B^x_a$ and $B^x_a \\approx_{\\eps} C^x_a$, then $A^x_a \\approx_{\\delta+\\eps} C^x_a$.\n   330\t\t\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:commutation-analysis-3}\n   331\t\t\tA^x_{a,\\,b}\\, C^x_{a,\\,c} \\ot \\Id_B \\approx_\\delta \\Id_A \\ot B^x_{a,\\,b,\\,c}\\,.\n   332\t\t\\end{equation}\n   333\t\tA symmetric argument gives\n   334\t\t\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:commutation-analysis-4}\n   335\t\t\tC^x_{a,\\,c}\\, A^x_{a,\\,b} \\ot \\Id_B \\approx_\\delta \\Id_A \\ot B^x_{a,\\,b,\\,c}\\,.\n   336\t\t\\end{equation}\n   337\t\tThe claim follows by subtracting \\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-3} and \\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-4}.\n   338\t\\end{proof}\n   339\t\n   340\t\\begin{lemma}[Sandwiched simultaneous measurement; modified from Fact 4.34 in \\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\\label{lem:ld-sandwich}\n   341\t\t\\uses{def:consistency, def:bracket, def:povm-conventions}\n   342\t\tLet $k \\ge 0$ be an integer and let $\\eps > 0$. Let $\\{A^{x,y_1,y_2}_{a_1,\\,a_2}\\}$ be a family of projective measurements with outcomes $(a_1, a_2) \\in \\mathcal R_1 \\times \\mathcal R_2$ such that for $i \\in \\{1,2\\}$,\n   373\t\t\\begin{equation}\\label{eq:pasting-1}\n   374\t\t\tA^{x,y_1,y_2}_{a_i} \\ot \\Id \\simeq_\\delta \\Id \\ot (G_i)^x_{[\\operatorname{eval}_{y_i}(\\cdot)=a_i]}\n   375\t\t\\end{equation}\n   505\t\\label{sec:types}\n   506\t\n   507\tThe question distribution of the Pauli basis test is \\emph{typed}: each question is a pair consisting of a type, drawn together with the other player's type from the edges of a fixed \\emph{type graph}, and a question content, drawn from a CL distribution determined by the pair of types.\n   508\t\n   509\t\\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear functions]\\label{def:typed-cl-functions}\n   510\t\t\\uses{def:cl-func}\n   511\t\tLet $\\mathcal T$ be a finite set (the \\emph{type set}) and let $V$ be $\\F^n$ for some integer $n \\ge 0$. Then the \\emph{graph distribution $\\mu_G$ of $G$} is the distribution over $U \\times U$ such that for every $(u,v) \\in U \\times U$,\n   519\t\t\\[\n   520\t\t\t\\mu_G(u, v) =\n   521\t\t\t\\begin{cases}\n   522\t\t\t\t1/(2m-k) & \\text{if } \\{u,v\\} \\in E\\,,\\\\\n   523\t\t\t\t0 & \\text{otherwise}\\,.\n   524\t\t\t\\end{cases}\n   525\t\t\\]\n   526\t\tThis is identical to the uniform distribution over ordered pairs $(u,v) \\in U \\times U$ such that $\\{u,v\\} \\in E$: each edge that is not a self-loop contributes two ordered pairs, and each self-loop contributes one, whence the normalization $2m-k$.\n   527\t\\end{definition}\n   528\t\n   529\t\\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear distributions]\\label{def:typed-cl-distributions}\n   530\t\t\\uses{def:typed-cl-functions, def:graph-distribution, def:cl-dist}\n   531\t\tLet $\\mathcal T$ be a type set and let $L = \\{L_u\\}_{u \\in \\mathcal T}$ and $R = \\{R_v\\}_{v \\in \\mathcal T}$ be $\\mathcal T$-typed families of conditionally linear functions on $V$. We state the quantum soundness of the classical game (Theorem~\\ref{lem:ld-soundness}, imported; see Remark~\\ref{rem:ld-soundness-provider}), the rigidity of the Magic Square game (Theorem~\\ref{thm:ms-rigidity}, imported), completeness of the Pauli basis test (Lemma~\\ref{lem:pauli-completeness}), and the main soundness theorem for the Pauli basis test (Theorem~\\ref{thm:pauli}), whose proof occupies Chapters~\\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}--\\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} and is completed in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}. The chapter closes with the qubit form of the soundness statement (Corollary~\\ref{cor:pauli-binary}) and the canonical parameter choice with its soundness bound (Definition~\\ref{def:introparams}, Lemma~\\ref{lem:delta-bound}).\n     7\t\n     8\tThroughout, the two players are denoted $\\mathrm A$ and $\\mathrm B$; for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$ we write $\\overline w$ for the other player. Games, strategies, values, conditionally linear (CL) functions and distributions, typed distributions sampled from the edges of a graph, and the state-dependent approximation $\\approx_\\delta$ between families of measurement operators are as in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the algebraic material on lines, canonical linear maps, the low-degree encoding, and generalized Pauli observables is from Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}.\n     9\t\n    10\t\\section{The classical low individual degree game}\n    11\t% Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.\n    12\t\\label{sec:ld-verifier}\n    13\t\\label{sec:ld-game}\n    14\t\n    15\tThe classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \\in \\F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \\in \\F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\\colon \\F_q^m \\to \\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.\n    16\t\n    17\t\\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\\label{def:ld-game}\n    18\t\t\\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}\n    19\t\tThe game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m,d,k \\in \\N$, $q \\in \\N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$. We write $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ to emphasize the dependence on the parameter tuple. The type set of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is\n    20\t\t\\[\n    21\t\t\t\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} = \\{\\mathsf{Point}, \\mathsf{ALine}, \\mathsf{DLine}\\}\\;,\n    22\t\t\\]\n    23\t\tand the distribution over type pairs $(t_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B})$ is uniform over $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} \\times \\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$. The ambient space is the direct sum $V = V_X \\oplus V_I \\oplus V_V$ of three register subspaces: the \\emph{point register} $V_X \\cong \\F_q^m$, the \\emph{coordinate register} $V_I \\cong \\F_q$, and the \\emph{direction register} $V_V \\cong \\F_q^m$. Elements of $V$ are identified with triples $(u,s,v) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q \\times \\F_q^m$. The question distribution and the win predicate of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ are specified in Definitions~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} and~\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} below.\n    24\t\\end{definition}\n    25\t\n    26\t\\begin{definition}[Question distribution of the classical low individual degree game]\\label{def:ld-question-distribution}\n    27\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:cl-func, def:cl-dist, lem:cl-concat, def:cl-canonical, def:line-representative}\n    28\t\tLet $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ be as in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-game}. Define $L_{\\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \\in V$,\n    29\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    30\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-ptf}\n    31\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\\;.\n    32\t\t\\end{equation}\n    33\t\tFor $s \\in \\F_q$, let $\\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that\n    34\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    35\t\t\t\\label{eq:chi-func}\n    36\t\t\ts = (\\chi(s)-1)\\,\\frac{q}{m} + r\n    37\t\t\\end{equation}\n    38\t\tfor some $0 \\le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\\{0,1,\\ldots,q-1\\}$ under the identification of $\\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Since $m$ divides $q$, when $s$ is uniformly distributed on $\\F_q$ the index $\\chi(s)$ is uniformly distributed on $\\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$. Define $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ by\n    39\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    40\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-alnf}\n    41\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \\bigl(L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\\, s,\\, 0\\bigr)\\quad\\text{for all } (u,s,v) \\in V\\;,\n    42\t\t\\end{equation}\n    43\t\twhere $i = \\chi(s)$ and $L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ denotes the canonical linear map with one-dimensional kernel spanned by $v$, used to compute canonical representatives of lines (Definition~\\ref{def:line-representative}). The function $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the concatenation (in the sense of Lemma~\\ref{lem:cl-concat}) of the $1$-level CL function projecting $V_I \\oplus V_V$ onto $V_I$ with the family of $1$-level CL functions $\\{L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}\\}$ on $V_X$ indexed by $i \\in \\{1,\\ldots,m\\}$; thus $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is a $2$-level CL function. Define $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ by\n    44\t\t\\begin{equation}\n    45\t\t\t\\label{eq:cl-dlnf}\n    46\t\t\tL_{\\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \\bigl(L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\\, s,\\, \\pi_{i-1}(v)\\bigr)\\;,\n    47\t\t\\end{equation}\n    48\t\twhere $i = \\chi(s)$ and $\\pi_{i-1}$ zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input. The function $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the concatenation of (i) the identity on $V_I$, (ii) for each $i$ the $1$-level CL function $v \\mapsto \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ on $V_V$, and (iii) for each pair $(s,v') \\in V_I \\oplus V_V$ the $1$-level CL function $L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{v'}$ on $V_X$; thus $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is a $3$-level CL function.\n    49\t\n    50\t\tThe question distribution of $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ is the typed CL distribution obtained as follows: sample a type pair $(t_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B})$ uniformly from $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}} \\times \\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$, sample $z = (u,s,v)$ uniformly from $V$, and send each player $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$ the question $(t_w, L_{t_w}(z))$.\n    51\t\\end{definition}\n    52\t\n    53\tThe next two lemmas show that the CL functions $L_{\\mathsf{Point}}$, $L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$, $L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ give rise to the axis-parallel and diagonal line-versus-point distributions.\n    54\t\n    55\t\\begin{lemma}\\label{lem:alnf}\n    56\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\n    57\t\tConsider the pair $(\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\bigl((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0)\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\ell = \\ell(u_0, e_i)$ where $i = \\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\F_q^m$, and $\\ell$ is a line that goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$.\n    58\t\\end{lemma}\n    59\t\\begin{proof}\n    60\t\t\\uses{def:line-representative}\n    61\t\tSince $s$ is uniformly random in $\\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$, the index $i = \\chi(s)$ is uniformly random in $\\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$, so $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\\ell(u_0,e_i)$. Since $u_0 = L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u)$ is the canonical representative of the line through $u$ in direction $e_i$, we have $u \\in \\ell(u_0,e_i)$.\n    62\t\\end{proof}\n    63\t\n    64\t\\begin{lemma}\\label{lem:dlnf}\n    65\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\n    66\t\tConsider the pair $(\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\bigl((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0)\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\ell = \\ell(u_0, v)$ where $i = \\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\F_q^m$, and $\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,m\\}$.\n    67\t\\end{lemma}\n    68\t\\begin{proof}\n    69\t\t\\uses{lem:alnf}\n    70\t\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\ell(u_0,\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\n    71\t\\end{proof}\n    72\t\n    73\t\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\label{def:line-point-dist}\n    74\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\n    75\t\tThe \\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. The \\emph{diagonal line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the distribution $\\mu_{L_{\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\ell = (u_0,s,v),\\, u)$. The \\emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\\mathsf{Line}}$ is the equal mixture of the two: with probability $\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\mathsf{ALine}}$, and with probability $\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\mathsf{DLine}}$.\n    76\t\\end{definition}\n    77\t\n    78\t\\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\\label{def:ld-win-predicate}\n    79\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:line, def:polyfunc}\n    80\t\tFix $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\n    81\t\t\\begin{itemize}\n    82\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\in \\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\F_q^k$.\n    83\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\colon \\F_q \\to \\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\n    84\t\t\t\\item Type $\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\in \\F_q^m \\times \\F_q \\times \\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\n    85\t\t\\end{itemize}\n    86\t\tThe win predicate $D^{\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\mathrm A}, x_{\\mathrm A}, t_{\\mathrm B}, x_{\\mathrm B}, a_{\\mathrm A}, a_{\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\n    87\t\t\\begin{enumerate}\n    88\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\mathrm A} = t_{\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\mathrm A} = a_{\\mathrm B}$.\n    89\t\t\t% The source phrases both clauses with \"the\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\n    90\t\t\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\n    91\t\t\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. The universal\n    92\t\t\t% quantification over t used here is the local correction; see the remark below.\n    93\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Axis-parallel line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\mathsf{ALine}$ and $t_{\\overline w} = \\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,k\\}$ and all $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t e_i$, where $i = \\chi(s)$.\n    94\t\t\t\\item (\\textbf{Diagonal line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\mathsf{DLine}$ and $t_{\\overline w} = \\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\in \\{1,2,\\ldots,k\\}$ and all $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$, where $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\chi(s)$.\n    95\t\t\\end{enumerate}\n    96\t\tThe game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the typed game with type set $\\mathcal T^{\\mathrm{ld}}$, the question distribution of Definition~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution}, and win predicate $D^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$.\n    97\t\\end{definition}\n    98\t\n    99\t\\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}\n   100\t\tThe source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \\in \\F_q$ such that $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \\pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\\ell(u_0, 0) = \\{u_0\\}$, every $t \\in \\F_q$ satisfies $x_{\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \\mapsto u_0 + t \\cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$.\n   101\t\\end{remark}\n   102\t\n   103\tThe soundness properties of the low individual degree game are expressed in terms of the following class of measurements.\n   104\t\n   105\t\\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]\\label{def:ld-meas}\n   106\t\t\\uses{def:polyfunc, def:polymeasurements, def:polynomials-degree}\n   107\t\tLet $\\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$). By Definition~\\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\\colon \\F_q^m \\to \\F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \\le q-1$; the parameter regimes of this chapter (Definition~\\ref{def:introparams} fixes $d = 1$, and admissibility gives $q \\ge 2$) always satisfy this. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\{G_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k}\\}$ such that for each $i \\in \\{1,\\ldots,k\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\colon \\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\to \\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\n   108\t\\end{definition}\n   109\t\n   110\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \\emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\n   111\t\n   112\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\n   113\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\n   114\t\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\n   115\t\t\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\n   116\t\tThere exists a function\n   117\t\t\\[\n   118\t\t\t\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}(\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\,(dmk)^a \\bigl(\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\bigr)\n   119\t\t\\]\n   120\t\tfor universal constants $a \\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\eps$ in the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\n   121\t\t\\[\n   122\t\t\tG^w \\in \\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\n   123\t\t\\]\n   124\t\ton $\\hilb_w$ for $w \\in \\{\\mathrm A,\\mathrm B\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\n   125\t\t\\begin{align*}\n   126\t\t\tA^{\\mathsf{Point},\\, u}_{a_1,\\ldots,a_k} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   127\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   128\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot G^{\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\ldots,a_k)]}\\;,\\\\\n   129\t\t\tG^{\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\ldots,a_k)]} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   130\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   131\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot B^{\\mathsf{Point},\\, u}_{a_1,\\ldots,a_k}\\;,\\\\\n   132\t\t\tG^{\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k} \\ot I_{\\mathrm B}\n   133\t\t\t&\\approx_{\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}}\n   134\t\t\tI_{\\mathrm A} \\ot G^{\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\ldots,g_k}\\;,\n   135\t\t\\end{align*}\n   136\t\twhere $\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}} = \\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}}(\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\ket{\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\in \\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\n   137\t\\end{theorem}\n   138\t\\begin{proof}\n   139\t\t\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\n   140\t\tLet $\\Sigma = \\F_q$ and let $\\code \\subseteq \\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\colon \\F_q \\to \\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\F_q$. We may assume $d < q$. In the opposite regime the statement is immediate: for $k \\ge 1$ and $d \\ge q$ the prefactor gives $\\delta_{\\mathrm{ld}} \\ge a\\,(dmk)^a\\, q^{-b} \\ge q^{a-b} \\ge 1$, while the quantity bounded in Definition~\\ref{def:povm-distance} never exceeds $2$ for families of POVM elements, so the three approximations hold for an arbitrary choice of $G^w \\in \\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$; and for $k = 0$ every answer tuple is empty, all measurements involved are single-outcome, and the approximations hold with error zero. For $d < q$, evaluation is injective on polynomials of degree at most $d$ and a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $d$ vanishes at no more than $d$ of the $q$ points, so $\\code$ is a linear $[q,\\, d+1,\\, q-d]_\\Sigma$ code.\n   141\t\t% The paper prints the parameters as [q, d+1, n-d+1] with an undefined n. With the\n   142\t\t% intended value n = q the printed distance q-d+1 exceeds the true minimum distance\n   143\t\t% q-d of the degree-d evaluation code, and the dimension claim d+1 requires d < q.\n   144\t\t% Both points are corrected above; the regime d >= q, which the parameter tuple of\n   145\t\t% Definition def:ld-game permits, is handled by the triviality argument.\n   146\t\tThe two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\\code^{\\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, coincides with the game $\\mathcal G^{\\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test. Theorem~4.7 of~\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, instantiated with its internal parameter $k$ chosen as $m^3 d$ (this parameter is unrelated to the simultaneity parameter $k$ of $\\mathsf{ldparams}$), therefore yields the present statement for $k = 1$.
